prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect, and for its experimental discovery in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: B048 remains my first choice after reading the full set of ballots. It is a discovery that sits at the centre of modern condensed-matter physics: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall state, which showed that band insulators carry a topological invariant that protects edge and surface states, and Molenkamp's group then observed the predicted helical edge transport in HgTe quantum wells. It has the full prediction-and-confirmation arc, about two decades of independent confirmation in transport, ARPES and other probes, and a stable interpretation. Five of six rankers who ranked it placed it in their top three, and it has the strongest opening support in the shortlist apart from the twisted-graphene candidate, which has a similar breadth of support but is younger. The theory-plus-experiment triple is a natural three-person configuration, so no artificial compression of credit is needed.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The credited triple leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal was what made Molenkamp's experiment a targeted test, and it leaves out the three-dimensional topological insulator work by Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and the early ARPES experiments. The Kane-Mele graphene model is also not the material realisation, because the spin-orbit gap in graphene is tiny. Finally, the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter covers neighbouring ground, so a reader could see this as a second helping of topology. If the committee judges the experimental credit to belong to the HgTe route, the HgTe proposal is a real gap that a three-name limit cannot close.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B048 third and argued that the omission of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction is the main attribution problem and that a fair prize would have to explain it.
responses.response: I agree that this is the sharpest problem and I do not think it can be waved away. My answer is that the Nobel citation can be worded around the discovery, namely the Z2 topological insulator and its first observation, rather than around every step of the HgTe route. Kane and Mele supplied the concept and the classification; the BHZ proposal is a specific material prediction that sits between theory and experiment, and Molenkamp's group both worked with it and carried out the measurement. That is a judgement about priority which I hold with some uncertainty. If Mehlig can show that BHZ was more than a materials recipe, I would be willing to rework the allocation, but the three-person ceiling means that one of the three would have to give way, and I do not see which.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B038) first, arguing that it is the architecture under essentially all superconducting quantum processors, while ranking B048 second and acknowledging that proximity to the 2025 prize is a timing question.
responses.response: I accept that B038 is original and influential, and I do not dispute the strength of the physics. But Johansson himself identifies two difficulties that weigh heavily with me: the allocation among four people (Blais, Girvin, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) cannot be cleanly separated into three, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits is very close in subject and in the community involved. Johansson also notes his own professional proximity to the field, which deserves to be weighed when we compare how strongly each of us ranks it. By contrast, B048 has a clean theory-plus-experiment split with no recent prize in the same technical area, so I stay with B048 as the stronger configuration.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked optical lattice clocks (B049) first, as a clear, original discovery that underpins the redefinition of the second, and ranked B048 third while noting that the 2016 topological prize reduces its priority.
responses.response: The lattice clock case is strong and I rank it among my own alternatives. Katori and Ye is a clean two-person credit and the maturity is good. On the point she raises against B048, I agree that the 2016 prize is related, but it honoured topological phase transitions and the Hall-type topological phases (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz); the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators and the spin Hall state are a distinct discovery with a separate experimental confirmation, and they are the part that led to the wide search for topological materials. I do not think the overlap is large enough to be disqualifying. My remaining hesitation about the clocks is whether the committee sees this as a discovery or as a measurement achievement that follows on from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-clock recognition.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B048 first on the grounds of a clearly bounded discovery with a theory-to-experiment chain, wide impact on materials physics, and stable interpretation after two decades of confirmation, while noting that the HgTe proposal and the 3D work complicate allocation.
responses.response: We agree on the scientific case and on the maturity. I would only add that her point about impact on materials characterisation and device concepts should be treated with some care in the citation: the prize should reward the discovery of the topological state and its observation, not downstream spintronics or topological quantum computing, which remain speculative. On allocation, we both flag the same gap, so on that we are not in disagreement; the disagreement is only about whether the gap is large enough to move the prize to a candidate like B016, where the theory-and-experiment pair is more compact but the field is younger.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked dynamical mean-field theory (B006) first as the standard non-perturbative framework for correlated electrons, and ranked magic-angle graphene (B016) second and B048 sixth, calling B048 significant but with credit overlap.
responses.response: DMFT is a method of lasting value and I can see why a solid-state colleague puts it first. My reservation is that its credit is spread across Metzner, Müller-Hartmann, Jarrell and Rozenberg as well as the three credited names, and as Mehlig also observes, its case rests on method rather than on a discrete discovery. That makes the attribution weaker than for B048, even though B048 has its own gap. On Eriksson's ranking of B016 above B048, I think this is a legitimate difference of weighting between a mature, well-confirmed discovery and a younger, faster-moving one, and I keep B016 as my first alternative rather than my preferred choice because the pairing mechanism is still unsettled.

uncertainties: Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal and the three-dimensional topological insulator work can be left outside the credited names without making the prize look incomplete.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases is judged close enough to count against a second topology prize.
Whether the committee would prefer the magic-angle graphene case (B016) now, given its comparable breadth of support, or wait for the pairing mechanism to be better understood.
My recollection of the history of the HgTe experiment and the early 3D work is from memory and is not independently verified in the supplied material.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, my early mentor Hector Rubinstein, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group; none is among the credited names for any shortlisted candidate. My own research is in string theory and cosmology, so I am a non-specialist in condensed matter and atomic physics, which I take into account when weighing attribution claims.
